title: Normal distribution: probabilities and unknown parameters
what_it_asks: You are given a normal model $X \sim \mathrm{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$, sometimes with $\mu$ or $\sigma$ unknown, plus some probabilities or percentiles. You find a probability with the calculator, or use an inverse normal z-value to find an unknown value, mean or standard deviation. The idea is that every normal probability links to a standardised value $z = \frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}$, and symmetry lets you move between tails.
typical_structure: Usually three or four parts, sometimes two or five, with about ten to thirteen marks in total. An early part is a plain probability or a short statement. A middle part uses inverse normal to find a value or one unknown parameter. A later part often needs two simultaneous equations for $\mu$ and $\sigma$, or feeds a probability into a binomial or test part. Later parts often rely on earlier results, sometimes signalled by "hence" or "given that".
mark_pattern: Three-mark parts are the most usual. Typical sequences are M1 A1 A1, M1 B1 A1 and M1 M1 A1. A one-mark part is usually a single B1 for a stated value or fact. In a standardising part, the first M1 is for setting $\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}$ equal to a z-value. The B1 is for the correct z-value from the inverse normal. A further M1 is for solving, and the last A1 is for the final value in the accuracy asked for. Simultaneous problems usually give a method mark for each equation, then a method mark for solving and accuracy marks for $\mu$ and $\sigma$. Show-that parts end with an A1 that needs a complete argument (cso).

where_marks_leak.text: This is a common loss. You round to the wrong number of decimal places or significant figures, or round a z-value early. The final A1 goes even though the method was right.
This is a common error. You use a positive z for a value below the mean when forming simultaneous equations. The equation is wrong, so the A1 is lost, and the method mark for solving may go with it.

You use the wrong tail or the wrong sign of z for a given percentage, such as using 0.9 when the probability is the upper tail 0.1. The M1 for the standardised equation is lost, and the accuracy marks after it.
You write $\frac{\mu - x}{\sigma}$ the wrong way round, or divide by the variance instead of $\sigma$. The M1 for the standardising equation is lost, and the A1 that depends on it.

write_to_earn: Sketch a quick normal curve, shade the region and mark the mean, so you choose the right tail and sign of z.
Write the standardised equation $\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma} = z$ with the z-value stated before you solve it.
For two unknowns, write both equations separately, then solve them together and state $\mu$ and $\sigma$ clearly.
Keep full calculator values through the working and round only on the final line to the accuracy asked.
In a show-that part, write the step just before the printed result, then the result.
check_before_you_leave: z sign matches the side of the mean
Earlier result carried into later part
